To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the iron storage protein bacteroferritin (BFRB) is central for bacterial iron homeostatis, that the BFRB-ferredoxin (bfd) protein-protein interaction is essential for the regulation of iron levels in the bacterial cell, and that small molecules designed to disrupt the interaction of BFRB with bfd can potentiate fluoroquinolones against Pseudomonas.
small molecule inhibitors of P. aeruginoga BfrB–ferredoxin (Fdx) interaction decrease bacterial fitness and potentiate fluoroquinolones activity.
we have identified small molecule probes designed as BfrB– Bfd interaction inhibitors, which are able to decrease P. aeruginosafitness and potentiate fluoroquinolones activity in vitro.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of small molecule inhibitors that target bacterial iron homeostatic proteins.
developing small molecule inhibitors of bacterial iron metabolism.
the development of novel small molecule probes of bacterial iron homeostases that may have potential utility as antimicrobial agents or adjuvants to existing antibiotics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study describes the first small molecules that inhibit the BfrB-Bfd interaction and that these molecules can be used to modulate the iron homeostasis of P. aeruginos.

we have developed a small molecule inhibitor that blocks the interaction of BfrB with its cognate ferredexin (Bfd) and this inhibitor is effective in combination with fluoroquinolones to kill P. aeruginosis cells.
we have designed a series of small molecule inhibitors that selectively target a bacterial protein–protein interaction that is essential to the mobilization of iron for bacterial growth and survival.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the BfrB protein–protein interaction represents an attractive target for the development of novel antibacterial agents.
the BfrB protein is a novel and promising antibacterial target.

we have designed and characterized small molecules that inhibit a protein–protein interface that is central to bacterial growth, and that this inhibition can potentiate the activity of an antibiotic that is commonly used to treat infections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 4-subtituted isoindoline-1-ones are potent inhibitors of the Bfd-BfrB interaction.
small molecule inhibitors of bacterial protein–protein interactions can be developed and used to modulate bacterial fitness.
the BfrB-Bfd interaction is a druggable target that can be exploited to potentiate the activity of existing antibiotics.
